--- title: "Testing the robustness of a published claim: the EU-frames case" author: "Pair: [names]" date: today format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 2 code-fold: false df-print: paged execute: message: false warning: false knitr: opts_chunk: fig-width: 8 fig-height: 5 --- ## The claim, and what we are doing to it The original author (OA) studied how citizens frame the European Union. One claim from their paper is our target: > "… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (Teney 2016: 619) Operationalised the way that the Multi100 project constrained it for its five analysts: does a country's **unemployment rate** (poor economic performance) lower the **cosmopolitan** dimension of EU framing (peace, democracy, free movement, cultural diversity, a stronger say in the world)? The published result was a coefficient of −0.0034, t = −4.03. You have the data, the tools and the workflow that the project used, and the code you work through is the coordinator's own submitted analysis. You are analyst no. 6, and the question is how robust that number is to *justifiable* alternative choices. Work through the five tasks below in order, from a setup check to two dots on the live class chart: an exploratory one from Task 4, and a declared one from Task 5, whose specification you fix in your preregistration before running it. ::: callout-tip ## How the tasks work Every task is a callout box with instructions, a **TODO** you complete, and code chunks that **already run** – so the report renders from the first preview. You edit the prose blanks and, in Tasks 4 and 5, the code. The course site also has a browser version of this exercise, for practice without an installation or as a fallback if your machine fails; this workspace is the full IDE pipeline. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 1 – Set up, and fix the vocabulary"} **First, the setup check.** If this report renders at all, your workspace is working: the packages are installed, the data are in place, and the helpers are loaded. Render it once now, before anything else. If it does not render, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` in the console – it names the packages you are missing and how to install them. **Then, before touching data, fix the vocabulary.** In the four scenarios below, three are doing one of our three Rs, while one is doing something else entirely. **TODO: read the four scenarios and fill in the gaps.** ***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer reruns the authors' Stata `.do` file on the authors' data and gets a *different* coefficient from the one printed in the paper. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though what they *tried* to do failed. ***Scenario 2:*** The analyst uses the authors' submitted replication dataset, but they re-implement the model in R instead of Stata and centre the predictor. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_? ***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team tests the identical hypothesis on a *separate, much larger* dataset chosen to be theoretically equivalent, and gets results that contradict the original. Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_. ***Scenario 4:*** Instead of the survey data used by the original authors, another researcher tests the same underlying idea on social-media texts using a machine-learning classifier method that the original never used. To their surprise, the authors' original findings prove \_\_\_\_\_\_ and the researcher concludes that they provide a reliable middle-range theory of the phenomenon they investigate. *(Answers: 1 reproducibility – the activity is reproducibility even though it failed to match, so the verdict is 'not reproduced'; 2 arguably still reproducibility, a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is a re-computation, though centring the predictor and differing estimator implementations nudge towards robustness; 3 replicability – same question, independent new data; 4 generalisability – the impostor, new data and a new method at once.)* ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 2 – Meet the panel"} The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is the country-year panel behind the whole exercise. It is already loaded as `euframes` in the setup chunk, and the copy in `data/` is byte-identical to the one published in the analyst's fork on OSF (osf.io/6zqct – "Multi100 \| Teney_EurSocioRev_2016 \| Analyst_C6HJR", main folder); the official Multi100 archival record is at osf.io/8rtwe. **TODO:** run the chunks, then read the small-multiples figure. Which countries trend down over 2004–2013? Note one in a comment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # How many countries, how many years, how big is the panel? euframes |> summarise( countries = n_distinct(cntry), years = n_distinct(year), rows = n() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: You should see **27 countries**, **10 years** (2004–2013), and **270 rows**. The outcome we care about first is `mcosmo` – the mean cosmopolitan framing of the EU in each country-year (a 0–1 scale). The predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate. The column `growth` is annual GDP growth, and `n_cy` counts the survey respondents behind each row. Every column is described in `data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(euframes, aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) + geom_line(colour = "grey55") + geom_point(size = 0.7) + facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013)) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean cosmopolitan framing (0–1)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mean cosmopolitan EU framing over time, by country – a version of OA's Figure 1.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cosmo-trend-1.png){#fig-cosmo-trend width=864} ::: ::: Most countries drift gently; a few move sharply around the 2009 crisis. That variation within each country over time is what the fixed-effects model in Task 3 uses. *Downloading from OSF (optional).* `R/get_data.R` fetches this file from the analyst's OSF fork the way that a researcher would, with a course-site mirror as a fallback. It is not needed – the file already ships in `data/` – but running it gives you practice in downloading a published file from its repository: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Optional: confirm data/EUframes_cy.csv from OSF (uses the local copy offline). source("R/get_data.R") ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 2, continued – name the estimand, draw the graph"} Before estimating, say *precisely* what you are estimating. An estimand has two parts: a **unit-specific quantity** and a **target population** (Lundberg et al. 2021). State it outside any model. **TODO – complete the estimand statement:** > Unit-specific quantity: the change in \[\_\_\_\_\] for a one-point difference in \[\_\_\_\_\]. Target population: \[\_\_\_\_\]. *(A defensible filling: the change in mean cosmopolitan framing within a country-year, for a one-percentage-point difference in that country's unemployment rate; across EU member states, 2004–2013.)* Next come the identification assumptions: the claims about what causes what that must hold for the coefficient to be read as the effect of unemployment. `R/dag_starter.R` builds the graph with `dagify()`, where every arrow is an ordinary R formula written the way you read a regression, effect on the left of the tilde and cause on the right. `framing ~ unemployment` is therefore the arrow unemployment → framing. The causal path and the two confounder pairs are switched on; the arguable arrows are in the same call, commented out with a `#`, each with a line of justification above it. Open the file, take the `#` off any arrow you believe, re-source, and re-run `adjustmentSets()`. A node appears in the plot only once some arrow mentions it, so the plot shows only the arrows that are switched on and the nodes that they join. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/dag_starter.R") plot_dag(dag) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The starter DAG: unemployment → framing, with country and year as confounders.](index_files/figure-html/dag-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # What must we adjust for to identify the unemployment -> framing effect? dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, exposure = "unemployment", outcome = "framing") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` { country, year } ``` ::: ::: For the starter graph the adjustment set is `{ country, year }`, which is what the two-way fixed effects that you fit in Task 3 absorb. Country fixed effects adjust for `country` and year fixed effects for `year`, so the DAG and the model encode the same identification claim. **TODO – answer two questions in a sentence each:** 1. What do **country** and **year** fixed effects adjust for, in plain terms? *(country-constant traits, and shocks common to all countries in a year)* 2. What can they **not** fix? *(a time-varying, country-level confounder – e.g. GDP growth moving both unemployment and framing within a country over time)* Whatever set is returned by your DAG becomes field 4 of the preregistration you write in Task 5. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 3 – Reproduce the recorded result"} This is the **reproducibility** check. Fit the two-way fixed-effects model that follows from the constraints of Task 2 in Multi100: cosmopolitan framing on grand-mean-centred unemployment, with country and year fixed effects. The target is **t = −3.804** (df = 233, N = 270) – the value on record for analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Grand-mean centre unemployment, as the submitted analysis did. With # two-way fixed effects this shifts the intercept, not the slope or the t – it # is the transformation that the constrained specification names, so do it # explicitly. euframes <- euframes |> mutate(unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp, na.rm = TRUE)) # fixest::feols – the bar separates the regression from the fixed effects. m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes) tidy(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-corrected .cell tbl-cap='The constrained model on EUframes_cy.csv.'} ```{.r .cell-code} modelsummary( list("two-way FE (fixest)" = m1), estimate = "{estimate}", statistic = "t = {statistic}", gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"), coef_rename = c("unemp_c" = "Unemployment (centred)") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
two-way FE (fixest)
Unemployment (centred) -0.003
t = -3.804
Num.Obs. 270
R2 0.754
``` ::: ::: The coefficient is **−0.00347** with **t = −3.804**, which is the value recorded for analyst C6HJR, reproduced from the published data and the published model. When two fixed-effect dimensions are present, `feols` reports classical (IID) standard errors by default, which assume that the errors are independent and identically distributed. That is why the *t* value matches, to three decimals, the value that the analyst obtained with `plm`. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reproduction and the five analysts"} You reproduced the recorded value exactly, and so did everyone else in the class, because everyone ran the same code on the same file. That is why reproducibility is the cheapest of the three Rs to establish. The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for the same claim, and came back with five different answers, one of them not significant. Their pipelines are competent, well-organised work, so the spread does not come from poor analysis. It arises because a claim stated in words leaves several defensible quantities open, and different analysts estimate different ones without noticing that they have chosen between them. In Task 2 you named the quantity you are after and drew the graph from which your adjustment set follows. In Task 4 you will see how far the answer moves when the other choices change. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 4 – Work the menu"} This task is **exploratory**. Try several specifications, see what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. The specification that you submit with `submit_exploration()` at the end of this task is labelled exploratory on the class chart. The one labelled declared is fixed later, in the preregistration cell of Task 5, before it is run. Both carry the tag that `submit_exploration()` prints, such as `amber-otter-42`, which is kept in the file `.class-tag` of this workspace and lets you find your own circles on the chart. To choose your own, write `submit_exploration(nickname = "...")` with a nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public. `try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the specification menu. Every argument defaults to the specification that you just reproduced, so changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays as it was in Task 3. Every call is a real fit on your machine. The Level 1 arguments change the question, the Level 2 arguments select which version of the country-year panel is fitted (which items the outcome was built from, whether its cells were weighted, what was done with respondents who mentioned nothing, which published series supplies the predictor), and the Level 3 arguments set the form of the predictor. The printout gives the slope `b` with its conventional standard error and *t*, the claim-aligned partial *r*, two p-values, the class of the result and its placement among the 864 specifications on the curve of the claim. The two p-values come from tests that allow the years of one country to be correlated with one another, which the conventional *t* does not. The first clusters the standard errors by country, with the CR2 correction that suits a small number of countries, and is read from `data/spec_curve.csv`. The second is the wild cluster bootstrap by country, which runs on your machine with each fit: it imposes the null of no association, flips the signs of the residuals country by country 9,999 times, and counts how often a *t* at least as large as the observed one arises. The bootstrap is the test that classes every point on the curve. The reproduced specification lies below zero, but with a bootstrap p of 0.110 it is not significant, and 67% of the 864 specifications lie further in the direction of the claim. The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. Every other option is still an argument of `try_spec()`, and trying one is part of the exercise: the helper refuses it, gives the reason why it is not on the curve, and names the page of the course site that teaches it. **TODO:** run the six calls below and the refused one after them, then write your own. It appears on the live class chart as an **exploratory** result: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} submit_exploration() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why label it 'exploratory'?"} You chose this specification after seeing what several of them do, so it lacks the guarantee carried by a choice that is fixed in a preregistration before it is run: it might have been chosen *because* of its result, and neither you nor anyone else can now rule that out. Almost no published paper reports which of its analyses were explored and which were planned. The class chart does, because everyone submits twice: once here, and once in Task 5 after preregistering a specification, so the two sets of dots can be read against each other. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 5 – My preregistration"} A preregistration fixes your specification **before** you know its result, which stops you from quietly picking the one that happens to give the answer you wanted. In a real study it is filed, with a date stamp, in a public registry such as the OSF. In this report the preregistration is the cell below, and the code enforces it: the R session keeps the choices that you set in that cell, every later cell reads them, and `build_model()` refuses model code that departs from them. Make one choice on each decision of the specification menu, then run the cell. The menu has fourteen decisions. The seven at Level 1 fix the question you are asking, the four at Level 2 fix how that question is measured, and the three at Level 3 fix how it is estimated. The curve of 864 specifications keeps two or more options on nine of these decisions and a single option on the other five, which are the sample, the weighting, the scoring rule, the model family and the inference. An option that is not on the curve stops `prereg()` with the reason why, as it stops `try_spec()`. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the course convention, applied automatically: the claim expects framing to rise with GDP growth, so the sign of a growth slope is flipped, and 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign for everyone. Task 2 of Multi100 fixed unemployment as the measure; the curve also holds GDP growth. In Task 1 of Multi100, where the choice was left to them, four of the five analysts already used GDP growth, two of them beside unemployment. ::: ::: {.callout-important title="How this block maps to a real preregistration"} *A real preregistration, shortened. Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). The claim I am testing: ................................................. # 2. Why these controls, in one DAG-grounded sentence: ....................... # 5. Supported if the claim-aligned coefficient is negative with bootstrap # p < .05; undermined if it is not significant or positive. I will # report what I get. prereg() # checks every choice against the menu and prints your preregistration ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DECLARED – your preregistered specification, fixed before the model is fitted: The question (Level 1) outcome : mcosmo predictor : unemp adjusted : nothing estimator : two-way fixed effects (country + year) sample : all whose average: none scored as : share The measurement (Level 2) no-opinion rule: zero items: all cells: unweighted series: wb_nat The estimation (Level 3) form: raw family: gaussian inference: wild cluster bootstrap by country claim_align: TRUE build_model(), run_spec() and report_result() read these choices from here. Rendered into your report, this cell is your preregistration, and it sits above the cells that fit and submit this specification. ``` ::: ::: An optional mirror form can be used to log preregistrations for the class, and the link to it is shared in the session. It is not required: the cell above, rendered into this report, is your official preregistration. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 5, continued – build, run and report"} This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part that your classmates cannot copy from you. Together, the class samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. Your specification is now fixed in the preregistration cell above, and the next step is to translate it into model syntax yourself.
